quotes.text: There were a few moments in Kiss' debut album when they tried to be artistic, but it was only too obvious that these guys weren't particularly good at it.
Since doing artistic things take time, and it was something not particularly worth doing anyway, they decided to concentrate on good old cock-rock for their sophomore release.
Kiss might have thought they were gods of rock, but... they struggled with the instrumental precision required to pull off hard-rock instrumentals.
It shows Kiss at its essence: dumb, catchy, and trashy. Its riffs are memorable, and they're also presented in a loose and rockin' manner.
Their songwriting chops are better than some people give them credit for, but their instrumental abilities were atrocious.
They were able to write a fair amount of catchy riffs, many of which are utterly dirty and perfectly trashy.
Peter Criss loved his R&B and Soul so that is why his Kiss Solo album gravitated towards those genres, but it is not what the Kiss fans wanted to hear and not this fan in particular.
Peter's direction makes sense for who he is and I get that now, but the songs here are too weak and not memorable or catchy for me.
An album full of demos and the band couldn't even spare the time to re-record them says a lot about this album.
I felt Paul's songs were mostly garbage as he was trying to be Bon Jovi instead of Kiss.
Kiss is not grunge, ever!! To make an album that follows the trend is always a recipe for disaster and that is what this is.
Kiss were chasing trends and not making them at this time. They wanted to be Bon Jovi when they should've concentrated on being Kiss which has been their problem for about a decade at this point.
The producer was Ron Nevison and I think he overproduced it. The keyboards were a little too much for me for a historically guitar driven band.
The real disappointment of this album is the fact it is not a full Kiss "Band" album.
I like to consider this a mini Paul Stanley solo album as he had to be the captain and steer the ship while his First Mate, Gene Simmons, had lost his way and his attentions were elsewhere.

Nothing about their music was as dark or ominous as their image might have suggested. It was about as Satanic as Simon & Garfunkel. If you listened to it without any idea what the band looked like, it was merely below average pop rock, with dumb, simplistic riffs that weren't all that catchy, brain dead choruses that weren't all that engaging, and lyrics that were too bad to be good but not bad enough to be fun.
Get past the image, and the music pretty much sucked.

Imagine the sleaze of Aerosmith without the cleverness, the loudness of The Who without the songcraft, the bombast of Led Zeppelin without the vision, the pomposity of Emerson, Lake, & Palmer without the musical chops to back it up – that's pretty much what you got with KISS.
it wasn't really live, they re-recorded pretty much everything in the studio and really only kept some of the drums and the crowd noise from Cobo Hall.

In the hands of Styles and his collaborators, all those pulsing synths and percolating drum machines do not add up to a transcendent experience. Kiss All The Time is 42 minutes of rhythms, textures, and vibes in search of a single compelling song. It is the sound of the nebulous concept of good taste being hollowed out into an empty vessel — a reverse "Emperor's New Clothes" situation where the clothes are the only thing there.
The album could have worked if there were hooks. Barring that, even some personality might have jolted these tracks to life. But Kiss All The Time is bereft of both melody and idiosyncrasy.

So it goes throughout most of the tracklist. The bass-bombed "Ready, Steady, Go!" is the kind of song an indie sleaze revival band in a Netflix drama might come up with, or maybe an actual post-peak 2000s dance-punk band buried deep on a late-season O.C. soundtrack. The shapeshifting "Season 2 Weight Loss" comes tantalizingly close to Hot Chip but lacks the pizzazz to leave an impression.
